reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Most intracranial aneurysms are saccular (berry) lesions arising at branch points of the circle of Willis, and many are asymptomatic until they rupture
Rupture causes aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, classically a sudden thunderclap headache described as the worst ever, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, and reduced consciousness
A non-contrast CT performed early is highly sensitive for subarachnoid blood; if negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia is used
An enlarging unruptured aneurysm can cause warning signs such as a painful third nerve palsy from a posterior communicating artery lesion
Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, family history, polycystic kidney disease, and connective tissue disorders
After rupture, priorities are securing the aneurysm by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping to prevent rebleeding, alongside management of complications
Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, and seizures are important complications after subarachnoid haemorrhage
Management of unruptured aneurysms weighs rupture risk (influenced by size, site, and morphology) against the risks of treatment, and small stable lesions may be monitored
reference.pathophysiology: A cerebral aneurysm is a focal outpouching of an intracranial artery wall, typically forming at bifurcations where haemodynamic stress is greatest and the muscular and elastic layers are relatively deficient. Over time, wall degeneration and turbulent flow allow the sac to enlarge. Rupture releases arterial blood into the subarachnoid space, abruptly raising intracranial pressure and irritating the meninges. Subsequent breakdown products can trigger arterial vasospasm days later, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia, while blood interfering with cerebrospinal fluid circulation can produce acute or communicating hydrocephalus.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of thunderclap headache (reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT head to detect subarachnoid blood
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia when CT is negative but suspicion persists
CT angiography or digital subtraction angiography to define aneurysm location and morphology
MRI/MR angiography for detection and follow-up of unruptured aneurysms
Monitoring of sodium, and transcranial Doppler or imaging for vasospasm after haemorrhage
redFlags: Sudden thunderclap headache suggesting aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage requiring emergency imaging
Reduced or fluctuating consciousness and focal deficit indicating a large bleed or rebleeding
New painful third nerve palsy as a warning sign of an enlarging or symptomatic aneurysm
Acute hydrocephalus or deterioration from delayed cerebral ischaemia after haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Unruptured aneurysms may remain quiescent, but rupture carries substantial mortality and morbidity, with many deaths occurring before or soon after hospital arrival; early securing of the aneurysm and management of vasospasm and hydrocephalus improve outcomes for survivors.
pitfalls: Dismissing a sudden severe headache as migraine and missing subarachnoid haemorrhage
Relying on a late CT alone, when sensitivity falls and lumbar puncture may be needed
Failing to secure a ruptured aneurysm promptly, risking early rebleeding
Overlooking delayed complications such as vasospasm, hyponatraemia, and hydrocephalus
management: Secure a ruptured aneurysm urgently by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping to prevent rebleeding
Give nimodipine to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm while maintaining euvolaemia
Provide neurocritical care with blood pressure control before securing, analgesia, and treatment of hydrocephalus with an external ventricular drain
Monitor sodium for hyponatraemia from cerebral salt wasting or SIADH and use transcranial Doppler to detect vasospasm
Risk-stratify unruptured aneurysms for surveillance imaging versus preventive treatment, and modify risk factors with blood pressure control and smoking cessation
Screen relatives and consider associated conditions such as polycystic kidney disease and connective tissue disorders
Refer to a neurosurgical and neuro-interventional team and arrange multidisciplinary rehabilitation for survivors
